issues.legal_issue: An FIR under investigation should not be quashed when the complaint, taken at face value, alleges the basic facts of an offence and the accused persons’ culpability requires investigation.
material_facts: The complainant alleged that documents relied on to claim title to land were forged and used as genuine in a civil suit and in dealings with government authorities.
The complaint alleged that the accused had assisted in fabricating or using the documents.
The genuineness of the documents and the accused persons’ involvement had not been established and were matters for investigation.
A civil suit concerning title to the land and relying on the documents was pending.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in quashing the FIR and the ongoing investigation. The appeal was allowed and the matter was left for investigation without any finding on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 226 of the Constitution, quashing an FIR during investigation is an exceptional remedy. A High Court should not quash proceedings if the complaint lays the factual foundation for an offence, or decide disputed facts and culpability before evidence is collected. The Court applied State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, Rajesh Bajaj v. State, NCT of Delhi, State of Madhya Pradesh v. Awadh Kishore Gupta, V.Y. Jose v. State of Gujarat, and Harshendra Kumar D. v. Rebatilata Koley.

predicates.f_ir_quash_petition_during_investigation: A party sought to quash an FIR while the police investigation was ongoing.
predicates.complaint_alleges_basic_offense_facts: The complaint described facts which, if accepted as true, provide the basic foundation for a criminal offence.
predicates.accused_culpability_requires_investigati: Whether the accused committed an offence depends on facts that have not yet been established through investigation.

issues.definition: When an FIR is challenged during investigation, the complaint alleges the basic facts of an offence, and the accused persons’ culpability still requires investigation, the FIR must not be quashed.

issues.legal_issue: The bar on prosecution for specified offences involving documents produced in court does not apply when the alleged forgery occurred before the document was produced in court.
material_facts: The alleged forged sale deeds were relied on in a civil suit to support a claim of title.
The alleged forgery was said to have occurred before the documents were produced in court; the documents were not alleged to have been forged while in court custody.
issues.conclusion: The bar in Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not apply, and it did not prevent the FIR or investigation in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to the specified offences only when they are committed in respect of a document after it has been produced or given in evidence in court and while it is in the custody of the court. The Court relied on the Constitution Bench decision in Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah, which approved Sachida Nand Singh v. State of Bihar.

predicates.forgery_allegation_case: The criminal case concerns an allegation that a document was forged.
predicates.alleged_forgery_preceded_court_productio: The alleged forgery occurred before the document was produced or given in evidence in court.

issues.definition: In a case alleging forgery, when the alleged forgery preceded the document’s production in court, the court-document cognizance bar does not apply.
